idiom_name: sealed interface + one struct per operation + a single Run type switch
implementation_notes: Go has no sum types and no exhaustive matching, so the algebra is hand-written: an interface `Op` sealed by an unexported method (`isOp()`), one struct per operation, and one `Run(op, ...)` function containing a `type switch`. The type switch is checked at runtime, not by the compiler, so the interpreter needs a `default` arm returning an error for anything it does not know - that arm plus a totality test is what keeps a growing algebra honest. Interfaces are open by default: with an exported marker method any package can add an operation and silently break every interpreter, which is why sealing via `isOp()` and keeping the operations in one package is the Go reading of a closed set. The alternative OO form (`Run` as a method on each node) is equally idiomatic but makes adding a new interpreter a change to every node.
pitfalls: The default arm is the only totality check Go offers: without it a new operation falls through to the zero value as a silent no-op, so it must return an error (and be tested).
An exported marker method leaves the algebra open - any package can implement it; seal with an unexported method and keep operations in one package.
Struct values are copied into the interface: embedding slices or maps re-introduces aliasing between the program and the interpreter, so treat op payloads as immutable by convention.
